newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FOCUS - Indonesia raises interest rates, hits stocks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Indonesia raises interest rates, hits stocks.

text.p: Indonesia raised interest rates sharply on Tuesday to halt speculation in the rupiah, but while the move bolstered the currency it hurt a fledgling recovery in stocks, traders said.

The rupiah pulled itself off a historic low of 3,045 against the dollar to trade at 2,885/2,900 at the end of the day in Jakarta after the central bank said it was raising rates of its bilateral certificates for maturities up to three months.

Dealers said the hike reflected the resolve of the central bank to maintain tight monetary policies in an effort to contain currency instability. It also made it more attractive for investors to hold funds in rupiah while making it expensive to borrow rupiah for speculation.
But the move hurt stocks, since it raised funding costs and would affect profitability of the banking sector.

"The rise in the interest rates has helped the currency but it hasn't done much for the stock market," said Tom Inglis, head of research for ING Barings in Jakarta. "Uncertainties in the currency and the interest rates will keep equities nervous."

The Jakarta composite index closed down 9.11 points, or 1.52 percent, at 590.53. Earlier it had swung to a high of 612.21 points as state institutions propped up the market after an early dive, brokers said.

Banking stocks were the hardest hit following the central bank's move, with blue-chips Bank Negara Indonesia and Bank Internasional Indonesia high among the losers on expectations that funds will be more expensive, brokers said.

"Players had expected the index to rebound slightly as many stocks had been oversold. The rate hikes, however, have forced them to step back and think a thousand times before making a decision to buy," one broker said.

Jakarta stocks have been extremely weak this month, falling more than 130 points, or over 18 percent, since August 1. They have tracked the weakness in the rupiah, which was floated last week after the central bank said it was difficult to defend the unit in the wake of sustained speculative attacks on South East Asian currencies.
At its 3,045 low, the rupiah had fallen more than 600 points, or 28 percent, against the dollar since the beginning of the year. But some dealers said it looked as if the corner had been turned.

"The central bank has done a good job of squeezing the market. Now carrying costs are too high and offshore is selling dollars," said Edwin Png, the head of the treasury department at Bank of America in Jakarta. "The tight money policy has worked so far. There is a good chance that market confidence is back."

"... things are starting to settle down. Certainly the rupiah at 3,000 is probably the low at the moment, and, to be honest, we are expecting it to start firming up by the end of this week and start to appreciate," Nicholas Bibby, an economist with Chase Manhattan Bank in Hong Kong, told Reuters Financial Television.
Nevertheless, the currency instability has taken a toll on the economy, other traders said. They said food prices were likely to rise within months as the effect of the weaker rupiah spreads.

"The higher cost of importing raw materials used to produce food items has to be passed on to the consumer," one commodities trader said. "We will be seeing an increase in the prices of items such as chicken, meat and noodles."
All of the wheat used in making noodles, popular as a snack or a meal among Indonesians who are moving away from rice as their incomes grow, is imported.
Indonesia, the world's fourth-most populous country with more than 200 million people, also imports corn and soymeal, which are used to feed poultry and cattle.
